POPS ADHD Learning & Life Map™

Understanding how ADHD affects everyday access, support and independence

A structured multi-informant questionnaire for children and young people aged 8–18 with a confirmed ADHD diagnosis, bringing together the child or young person’s experience, home information and school information.

What this questionnaire is designed to understand

It looks beyond whether a child can or cannot do something. It examines when a skill is accessible, what makes access easier or harder, how much support is currently needed, and what the child may be ready to learn to manage more independently.

The child, parent/carer and school staff can contribute separately. Differences between viewpoints are treated as useful information about context, support and expectations rather than as errors.

Core principle: the aim is not simply to increase compliance. The aim is to understand the circumstances, differentiation, adult support and systems that allow the child to function more successfully and develop appropriate independence over time.
Also available: the book POPS ADHD Learning & Life Map™ is available as a companion resource for families, schools and professionals who want a fuller explanation of the framework and how to use it in practice.
Designed for current versions of Safari, Chrome, Edge and Firefox on computers and tablets.

Integrated ADHD Learning & Life Map™

Child / young person details

1. The child or young person’s view

This section shows what the child says is difficult, what helps, what adults sometimes do that makes things easier or harder, and what they would like to become better at doing for themselves. Their view matters because successful support should make sense to the child as well as to adults.

Parent/carer priorities and reasons

This section records the three areas the parent/carer most wants to work on at home. The explanation under each priority shows what the difficulty looks like in everyday life, what support is currently needed, and why improving it would matter.

These priorities are not automatically treated as the only important areas. They are used alongside the questionnaire results to make the action plan more relevant and manageable.

2. Functional profile: where support is most needed

This section brings together the child, home and school responses across each area. The percentage is not an exam score and it does not diagnose severity. A higher percentage means that, across the questions asked, this area currently involves more difficulty, more dependence on support, or less independent use of helpful strategies.

The short pattern statement underneath each score explains why the score is high. For example, the child may have the skill but only under certain conditions, may rely heavily on adult support, or may understand a strategy but not yet use it independently.

3. Where everyone sees a similar pattern

When the child, parent/carer and school give similar answers, we can be more confident that the difficulty is showing up across settings rather than only in one particular place. This does not mean the problem looks exactly the same everywhere, but it suggests that the underlying need is likely to be important across daily life.

4. Where home, school and the child see things differently

Differences are useful. They may show that the child can access a skill in one setting but not another, or that one setting is providing more structure, support, predictability, adult help or motivation. Each bullet below should therefore be read as a clue about what is different in the environment or support, not as evidence that one person is wrong.

5. Functional Access Map™: what helps and what gets in the way

This section focuses on conditions. It asks: When is the child more able to access the skill, and when does access drop? This is especially important in ADHD because performance can vary greatly with interest, task clarity, fatigue, stress, adult support, sensory load and how much information must be held in mind.

6. Development and independence: how much support is still doing the work?

This section looks at who is currently carrying the thinking, organising and self-management load. For example, is the child planning the task, remembering the steps, noticing overload and choosing a strategy themselves, or are adults still doing some of that work?

This matters because a child may complete a task successfully because the support is effective. Success with support is not the same as being able to do the same thing independently.

How to use this section: keep support that is clearly helping. Teach one small part of the process at a time. Only reduce support when there is evidence that the child can manage that part reliably.

7. Main area to work on first, and the next area to keep in mind

Rather than calling these “primary” and “secondary”, this report identifies:

Main focus now — the area most likely to give the biggest practical benefit if support is improved first.

Next area to watch — another important area that may be making the main difficulty harder, but which should not overload the plan with too many changes at once.

8. Coordinated action plan: what adults will change and what the child will learn

What is the purpose of this plan?

The plan works in two directions at the same time.

Adults and systems change first: parents and school change the task, environment, timing, prompts or structure so the child can access the skill more successfully now.

The child develops next: the child is helped to notice what is happening, understand what helps, practise one useful strategy and gradually take on more of the process when ready.

The aim is not to make the child independent as quickly as possible. The aim is to improve access now, reduce unnecessary stress and prompting, and build appropriate independence over time.

9. First shared test: checking whether our explanation is right

This section turns the report into a practical test. The aim is to change one important condition and see whether the child’s access improves. At the same time, the child practises one small matching skill.

This is not a reward chart and it is not a test of whether the child is trying hard enough. It is a way of checking whether our current explanation of the difficulty is useful. If the plan helps, we keep or build on it. If it does not, we change the explanation and try something different.

10. Review and revisit plan

Why review the plan?

The first plan is a working hypothesis. At review, home, school and the child look at what actually changed. A support can be kept, adjusted, simplified, strengthened, or stopped. The important question is not “Did the child behave better?” but “Did the support improve access, reduce unnecessary adult prompting, reduce stress, or increase appropriate independence?”

Saveable PDF: use the Download PDF button below. The report and anything typed into the review boxes will be included in the printed/PDF version.

11. Complete questionnaire record

This section contains the full information entered into the questionnaire. It is included so that important detail is not lost when the earlier sections summarise patterns. It records the biographical information, the contributors who took part, the child’s selected priorities, parent/carer and school priorities, selected supports, levels of adult support, and every question and answer from each completed contributor section.

13. Submit the completed questionnaire to POPS UK Office

One genuine submission button

When the questionnaire is complete, select Submit completed questionnaire to POPS. The questionnaire will prepare the structured report data and styled PDF, then securely send both files directly to the POPS submission service.

The submission service can then:

  • email the completed PDF and JSON data file to popsUKoffice@gmail.com;
  • send a copy to the parent/carer and school contributor where they have taken part;
  • retain the structured JSON for automated professional report generation;
  • optionally save a copy to the POPS Google Drive submission folder.

No native email app is required. The person completing the questionnaire does not need to download files, paste report text, or manually attach anything. After pressing Submit, this page moves directly to the POPS confirmation screen. No setup or email configuration is required from the person completing the questionnaire.
